# Voice profile — eff-mullin

## 1. Cadence

Sentences vary in length with a deliberate pattern: a longer sentence or two builds context, lists a bill's mechanics, or acknowledges a counterargument, and then a short sentence lands the verdict — 10/11 samples. From `californias-ab-412-still`: *"That may seem straightforward. In practice, it's anything but."* From `gay-bars`: *"This was not simply checking IDs at the door. PatronScan was building a database."* From `kids-online-safety`: *"When the safest legal option is to delete a forum, platforms will delete the forum"* — used twice in that piece, spaced paragraphs apart, as a refrain.

If a paragraph has been building toward a conclusion, cut the last sentence to under ten words and strip qualifiers. That short sentence is the point.

Parenthetical spans run throughout all 11 samples — ([measurement:round-parenthetical-spans] count: 97, 12.03 per 1,000 words) — used to slip in bill citations, inline definitions, and acknowledging context without diverting the argument: *"The registration system is a cumbersome beast at best—neither machine-readable nor accessible, it's more like a card catalog than a database—that doesn't offer information sufficient to identify all authors of a work"* (`californias-ab-412-bill`). When a parenthesis appears, it carries a citation or a definitional aside; it is not used for asides that express emotion.

Em-dashes appear in 10/11 samples ([measurement:em-dashes] count: 53, 6.57 per 1,000 words, several times per piece), most often to set off an appositive mid-sentence or to pivot between a premise and its consequence. En-dashes appear in 1/11 samples only and are not a stable pattern.

## 2. How a piece opens

Nine of eleven pieces open by naming the specific legislation within the first sentence and immediately characterizing it, not describing it neutrally — 9/11 (`congress-rushed`: *"In a voice vote earlier this week, the House of Representatives passed H.R. 6028, the 'Legislative Branch Agencies Clarification Act.'"* The next sentence explains why that framing is wrong.) The shortest opens with a claim alone: `court-records` — *"Court records belong to the public."*

Seven of eleven pieces use a concession structure in the first two sentences — 7/11 — granting the bill's stated purpose before turning sharply against it. From `californias-ab-412-bill`: *"At first glance, this might sound like a reasonable step toward transparency. But it's an impossible standard..."* From `no-fakes`: *"The NO FAKES Act is supposed to target harmful AI-generated impersonations. But in reality, it will make it easier to suppress commentary, satire, and other lawful speech."* Open with what the bill claims to do, then pivot in the same breath.

## 3. How a piece closes

Eight of eleven pieces close with a direct imperative addressed to a named institution — 8/11. The form is *Congress / The Senate / Lawmakers / These businesses should [verb]*. From `congress-rushed`: *"The Senate should reject H.R. 6028. The Copyright Office should serve the public—not presidential administrations, and not industry lobbyists."* From `kids-online-safety`: *"Lawmakers should reject it, and fast."* The final sentence is shorter than the one before it. End on the instruction, not on the reasoning.

Two pieces append a standalone action-call paragraph after the argument closes, directing California residents to contact legislators via link — 2/11 (`californias-ab-412-bill`, `californias-ab-412-still`). These appear to be a template element added to California-specific posts.

## 4. Who is being addressed, and how

The writing argues as an institution. First-person plural (*we*, *our*, *us*) carries the EFF voice in 10/11 samples ([measurement:first-person-plural-family] count: 19, 2.36 per 1,000 words, once or twice per piece): *"EFF opposed this bill from the start"* and *"we hope the Senate promptly rejects this bill"* (`california-ab-412-stalls`). This is organizational, not collegial — the *we* names EFF's position, not a shared experience with the reader.

First-person singular (*I*, *me*, *my*) appears in only 2 of 11 samples ([measurement:first-person-singular-family] count: 2, 0.25 per 1,000 words). The author does not appear as a person. Do not write *I*.

Second person (*you*, *your*, *you'll*, etc.) appears in 5/11 samples ([measurement:second-person-family] count: 11, 1.36 per 1,000 words) and is reserved entirely for action-call paragraphs — *"If you are a California resident and want to speak out about A.B. 412, you can find and contact your legislators"* (`californias-ab-412-bill`). Outside that context, drop second person.

Claims are stated flatly, without hedging — 8/11 samples: *"That simply isn't true."* *"It isn't true."* *"That's not theoretical."* (`californias-ab-412-still`, `kids-online-safety`, `chatbot-act`). No softening with *perhaps*, *it could be argued*, or *some might say*. When EFF has a position, the sentence names it.

Rhetorical questions appear in 4/11 samples ([measurement:question-marks] count: 9, 1.12 per 1,000 words, once or twice in the pieces that use them). They are always in setup position, answered immediately: *"Can teens discuss addiction and recovery? Can a 15-year-old post that she's worried she has a friend who is drinking too much?"* (`kids-act`). Do not leave a question hanging.

Named opponents are specific in 10/11 samples — Big Tech, Apple, X, TikTok, Meta, PatronScan — named rather than abstracted into "some companies." Allies are acknowledged via hyperlinks rather than sustained quotation; the argument is primarily EFF's own.

No personal biography appears anywhere in the corpus — 11/11. The author's age, history, and experience are absent; the only self-reference is institutional.

## 5. Figures

Functional metaphors drawn from legal and political conflict appear in 6/11 samples. Counting the following terms used non-literally as characterizations of legislation, systems, or their effects — *smokescreen*, *dragnet*, *death sentence*, *weaponize*, *sleight-of-hand*, *heckler's veto*, *vault* (modifying personal data or information), *troll* or *trolls* (in *copyright troll/trolls*), and *beast* (modifying a system or institution) — across all 11 samples: 10 instances, 1.24 per 1,000 words. Once or twice per piece in the samples that use them.

From `kids-online-safety`: *"legislative sleight-of-hand: an undefined concept given legal teeth."* From `no-fakes`: *"a 'heckler's veto' over legal speech."* From `californias-ab-412-bill`: *"For a small startup, throwing on such an impossible requirement could be a death sentence."*

These metaphors are short, borrowed from conflict and pressure, and landed without elaboration. They do not come from nature, the body, or literature. Do not reach for extended simile or fresh coinage — a one-word charge term placed precisely does more than a constructed figure.

## 6. Register range

The corpus shows a single register throughout: formal advocacy prose kept readable by contractions. Contractions appear in all 11 samples ([measurement:contractions] count: 86, 10.66 per 1,000 words, throughout): *"it's an impossible standard"*, *"they're far from the only ones"*, *"that's not theoretical."* Against them, uncontracted negatives coexist in 9/11 samples ([measurement:uncontracted-negatives] count: 32, 3.97 per 1,000 words, several times per piece): *"Congress should not extend"*, *"courts should not rush"*, *"the bill does not directly ban."* The split is roughly 86 contracted to 32 uncontracted. Uncontracted forms tend to appear in statements about legal obligation or formal recommendation; contracted forms appear in characterization and analysis. Use both. Do not normalize entirely to one form.

## 7. What the corpus never does

No profanity appears anywhere in the corpus — 11/11 samples ([measurement:profanity-vulgarity] count: 0, 0.00 per 1,000 words). The maximum expressive charge the writing delivers is carried by the functional metaphor vocabulary above (10 instances, 1.24 per 1,000 words): charge terms like *dragnet* and *weaponize* occupy the register where a different writer might reach for profanity. Use them at that rate; do not exceed it, and do not add profanity.

Subheadings, where they appear, make arguments rather than describe topics — 9/11 samples. Pieces without subheadings are the two shortest in the corpus. Where headings do appear, every one is a claim: *"A.B. 412 Is A Gift to Big Tech"*, *"This Bill Was Rushed Through"*, *"The Senate Should Stop This Bill"* (`californias-ab-412-bill`, `congress-rushed`). No heading in the corpus is neutral: there is nothing equivalent to "Background," "What the bill does," or "Summary." If you write a subheading, make it a verdict.

## 8. What this profile could not determine

The voice card was empty; every observation is derived from the corpus alone.

The corpus shows a single register (EFF advocacy blog posts about technology legislation). Nothing here shows how this voice behaves in correspondence, longer-form analysis, neutral reporting, or any register outside active legislative opposition.

Four observations were considered and dropped for insufficient support across samples: a claim about closing sentences using parallel three-part constructions, a claim about em-dashes appearing specifically at sentence-ends rather than mid-sentence, a claim about rhetorical questions occurring in groups of three, and a claim about sentence-initial *And* used for rhetorical emphasis. Each appeared clearly in one sample but not reproducibly across the corpus.

The en-dash count (7 instances in 1 of 11 samples) is not treated as a pattern.
